items.prompt: Tom copies slides verbatim into a 45-page document. Priya writes six short notes in her own words. Six months later, why is Priya's note more useful even though it's much shorter?
choices: It covers more of the original material
It states why the idea mattered to her, which makes it fast to recall and reuse
It was written faster than Tom's copy
It contains more exact quotes from the instructor
items.explanation: Priya's note isn't more complete than Tom's copy — it's actually a narrower claim. What it has that Tom's doesn't is a connection to something meaningful to her (the Kessler contract), which is what makes reading it later fast instead of like reading it for the first time.
items.reference:
📄 Copy-paste note — accurate, but reading it later feels like starting from zero
🗒️ Own-words note — narrower, but already states why it mattered
Why: processing an idea into your own words is what makes it fast to recall later — accuracy alone doesn't.

items.prompt: A note that is a verbatim copy of its source is described in this unit as low-value even when it's completely accurate. Why?
choices: Copying is slower than summarizing
Verbatim copies are usually inaccurate
The act of copying doesn't require actually processing the idea, so reading it later is close to reading it for the first time
Copied notes take up more storage space
items.explanation: Accuracy isn't the issue — a copy can be perfectly accurate and still be low-value, because copying it never required you to process what it meant. Processing (own-words rewriting) is a separate step from capture, and it's the one that actually pays off later.
items.reference:
📄 Copy-paste note — accurate, but reading it later feels like starting from zero
🗒️ Own-words note — narrower, but already states why it mattered
Why: processing an idea into your own words is what makes it fast to recall later — accuracy alone doesn't.

items.prompt: What does rewriting a raw capture in your own words actually add, if the original source already said the same thing more precisely?
choices: It adds a personal connection (why it mattered to you) that makes the note faster to recall and use later
It makes the note more technically precise than the source
It removes the need to ever look at the source again for any reason
It guarantees the note will never be misremembered
items.explanation: Own-words rewriting usually loses some precision compared to the source — that's fine. What it gains is a link to something meaningful to you, which is what future-you actually needs to recall and use the idea quickly.
items.reference:
📄 Copy-paste note — accurate, but reading it later feels like starting from zero
🗒️ Own-words note — narrower, but already states why it mattered
Why: processing an idea into your own words is what makes it fast to recall later — accuracy alone doesn't.

items.prompt: Priya's in-the-moment capture during the talk is just four words and a question mark. What is the capture step supposed to optimize for?
choices: Completeness — capturing every detail the source states
Speed and low friction, so the habit survives the moment it happens in
Correct grammar and full sentences
Immediately filing it into the right category
items.explanation: Capture is the step with the least available time — mid-talk, mid-conversation, on a commute. If it demands completeness or polish, people stop doing it. Completeness and polish are what the later processing step is for.
items.reference:
⚡ Capture — seconds, rough, incomplete is fine
🛠️ Process — minutes, later, this is where polish belongs
Why: a capture step that demands completeness gets skipped in the moments it's needed most.

items.prompt: Why does this unit treat capture and processing as two separate steps rather than one combined step done at the moment of learning?
choices: Because processing requires software that isn't available during a talk
Because combining them makes capture too slow for the low-friction moments it needs to happen in, so people stop capturing at all
Because separating them is required by most note-taking apps
Because processing must always happen exactly 24 hours after capture
items.explanation: The two steps have very different friction requirements. Capture has to be near-instant to survive real moments (mid-talk, mid-meeting); processing can take a few minutes because it happens later, on your own schedule. Merging them forces capture down to processing's slower pace, and capture is what gets skipped.
items.reference:
⚡ Capture — seconds, rough, incomplete is fine
🛠️ Process — minutes, later, this is where polish belongs
Why: a capture step that demands completeness gets skipped in the moments it's needed most.

items.prompt: What problem does linking a note to related notes actually solve?
choices: It makes notes easier to delete later
It gives the note a path back to you other than remembering its exact wording and searching for it
It makes each individual note longer and more detailed
It replaces the need to write the note in your own words
items.explanation: Without links, the only way to find a note again is to remember it exists and search for the right keyword — which is exactly what fails for Tom. A link lets you stumble onto a note by following a trail from something you were already looking at.
items.reference:
🔗 Linked note — found via a trail from a related note you were already reading
🔍 Unlinked note — found only by remembering it exists and searching the right keyword
Why: a real need for an old idea usually shows up connected to something else, not as a keyword you remember to search.

items.prompt: A 'second brain' note collection is described as more than a list. What makes it more than a list?
choices: It has more notes in total than a simple list would
The notes are connected to each other, so one note can lead you to others you'd forgotten you had
It automatically deletes notes that are never reopened
Every note is exactly the same length and format
items.explanation: Volume isn't what makes a collection a 'second brain' — connections are. A web of linked notes lets you rediscover things you'd forgotten by following a trail, which a flat list (however large) can't do.
items.reference:
🔗 Linked note — found via a trail from a related note you were already reading
🔍 Unlinked note — found only by remembering it exists and searching the right keyword
Why: a real need for an old idea usually shows up connected to something else, not as a keyword you remember to search.

items.prompt: Tom's 45-page document technically contains the answer he needs six months later, but he never finds it. What's missing?
choices: The document isn't long enough
A path back to the relevant note other than remembering the right keyword to search for
A table of contents listing every slide title
A backup copy stored somewhere else
items.explanation: Tom's document has the fact, but no connective structure — no link from anything else leads to it, so the only route in is search, and search over an unprocessed dump is slow and noisy. Presence in the document isn't the same as being findable.
items.reference:
🔗 Linked note — found via a trail from a related note you were already reading
🔍 Unlinked note — found only by remembering it exists and searching the right keyword
Why: a real need for an old idea usually shows up connected to something else, not as a keyword you remember to search.

items.prompt: A note system that requires every note to be assigned a folder, three tags, and a full cross-reference table at the moment of capture risks which failure mode?
choices: The notes will be too short to be useful
The friction is high enough that capture itself stops happening
The notes will be too accurate to be useful
It will run out of storage space quickly
items.explanation: This is the opposite failure from Tom's copy-paste trap: organizing too heavily at the moment of capture adds friction exactly where friction is most likely to kill the habit. A system that's technically more organized but gets abandoned within a week is worse than a looser one that's still in use six months later.
items.reference:
📥 Too passive — capture everything, process/link nothing (Tom's trap)
🗂️ Too heavy — organize so much at capture time that you stop capturing
Why: a working system sits between these — fast capture, lightweight processing done later.

items.prompt: Two note systems both fail, but in opposite ways: one captures everything and organizes nothing, the other organizes heavily but people stop capturing within a week. What do these two failures have in common?
choices: Both end with a note collection that isn't actually useful later, despite the effort put in
Both are caused by using the wrong note-taking app
Both only affect notes about technical topics
Neither failure is avoidable in practice
items.explanation: Both are real failure modes of the same underlying trade-off between capture and organization — too little organization leaves an unusable pile, too much organization kills the habit before any notes accumulate. Either way, the result is a system that doesn't hold up.
items.reference:
📥 Too passive — capture everything, process/link nothing (Tom's trap)
🗂️ Too heavy — organize so much at capture time that you stop capturing
Why: a working system sits between these — fast capture, lightweight processing done later.

items.prompt: Which of these counts as a note 'resurfacing,' according to this unit?
choices: Only a scheduled weekly review where you reread every note
Following a link from a related note you're already reading, rereading it when a new problem reminds you of it, or a periodic review — any of these
Only search results returned by typing an exact keyword
Only the moment a note is first written
items.explanation: Resurfacing isn't tied to one specific mechanism — a link, a triggered rereading, or a scheduled review pass all count, as long as the note actually gets encountered again at a useful moment. What matters is that some path back to it exists and gets used.
items.reference:
🔗 Following a link from a related note
💭 Rereading because a new problem reminded you of it
📅 A periodic review pass
Why: any path back to a note at a useful moment counts as resurfacing — it doesn't require a formal ritual.

items.prompt: A note was written accurately, processed into the writer's own words, and never encountered again by anyone, ever. According to this unit, how much value did it provide?
choices: Full value, because it was well written
Zero — a note that never resurfaces provided no value no matter how well it was written
Partial value, proportional to how much effort went into writing it
It's impossible to write a note that's never resurfaced
items.explanation: The unit is explicit on this: a note that sits unread forever provided zero value, regardless of how accurate or well-processed it was. Quality of writing and actually being found later are separate questions, and only the second one determines real-world value.
items.reference:
🔗 Following a link from a related note
💭 Rereading because a new problem reminded you of it
📅 A periodic review pass
Why: any path back to a note at a useful moment counts as resurfacing — it doesn't require a formal ritual.

items.prompt: Priya's system doesn't include a formal 'review every note weekly' ritual, yet her notes still resurface regularly. How?
choices: She has memorized every note she's ever written
Mostly through links between notes, triggered by whatever she's already looking at for an unrelated reason
Her notes app resurfaces a random note automatically each morning
She only writes notes she's confident she'll never need again
items.explanation: Resurfacing doesn't require a scheduled ritual — Priya's links do the work instead, surfacing old notes as a side effect of looking at something else related. That's still resurfacing; it's just triggered by need rather than by a calendar.
items.reference:
🔗 Following a link from a related note
💭 Rereading because a new problem reminded you of it
📅 A periodic review pass
Why: any path back to a note at a useful moment counts as resurfacing — it doesn't require a formal ritual.

items.prompt: In the capture → process → link → resurface loop, why does 'process' come before 'link' rather than after it?
choices: Because linking software requires the note to already be in its own-words form before it can be searched for related notes
Order doesn't actually matter between these two steps
Because linking always happens weeks after processing
Because capture and link are actually the same step
items.explanation: You need the note in its processed, own-words form to actually recognize what it relates to — a raw, uninterpreted fragment like 'anchor first even if rough - Kessler??' doesn't yet clearly connect to anything until you've worked out what it means. In practice the unit treats processing and linking as happening in the same short pass, but processing has to conceptually land first.
items.reference:
Capture→Process→Link→Resurface
Why: each step depends on the one before it — you can't usefully link a fragment you haven't yet worked out the meaning of.

items.prompt: Why is 'resurface' the last step in the loop rather than something that happens automatically once a note is written?
choices: Because resurfacing is optional and most notes never need to resurface
Because writing a note doesn't create a path back to it by itself — that path only exists if processing and linking were done first
Because resurfacing only applies to notes taken during formal courses
Because the loop is purely theoretical and doesn't apply to real note systems
items.explanation: A note existing and a note being findable are different things. Resurfacing is the payoff step, but it depends entirely on whether the earlier steps built a path back to the note — a raw, unprocessed, unlinked capture has no such path, which is exactly Tom's failure.
items.reference:
Capture→Process→Link→Resurface
Why: each step depends on the one before it — you can't usefully link a fragment you haven't yet worked out the meaning of.

items.prompt: The diagram shows an arrow labeled 'reinforces' looping from Resurface back to Process. What does this loop represent?
choices: That every note must be reprocessed every time it's resurfaced
That encountering a note again can prompt refining or strengthening the own-words version, which then makes future resurfacing easier
That resurfacing and processing are actually the same step
That the loop is a one-time process that never repeats
items.explanation: The loop isn't strictly linear in practice — finding a note again is often the moment you notice it could be phrased more usefully, or linked to something new. That optional reinforcement makes the note even easier to find next time, without requiring it on every single resurfacing.
items.reference:
Capture→Process→Link→Resurface
Why: each step depends on the one before it — you can't usefully link a fragment you haven't yet worked out the meaning of.

items.prompt: In the L2 comparison table, the copy-paste note and the own-words note describe the same fact about anchoring. What's the actual difference in what's written down?
choices: The copy-paste note is longer and more detailed
The own-words note ties the fact to a specific real situation and states why it mattered, while the copy-paste note states the fact in the abstract
The own-words note is factually more complete than the copy-paste note
There is no real difference — both are equally fast to use later
items.explanation: The own-words version is actually a narrower claim than the instructor's original — it drops the 'studies show' framing entirely. What it adds is the connection to the Kessler contract and why the idea mattered, which is what makes it fast to use six months later.
items.reference:
📄 Copy-paste — the fact, stated abstractly
🗒️ Own-words — the fact, tied to a real situation and why it mattered
Why: recall speed later depends on the connection to something meaningful, not on how completely the fact was stated.

items.prompt: Per the L2 comparison table, why is the copy-paste note slower to use six months later even though it states the fact correctly?
choices: Because reading it requires reconstructing why it mattered, since that connection was never written down
Because copy-pasted notes are always formatted badly
Because copy-pasted notes are usually inaccurate by the time they're reread
Because it takes longer to physically read a direct quote than a paraphrase
items.explanation: The copy-paste note has the fact but not the 'why it mattered to me' connection — so using it later requires reconstructing that link from scratch, which is slow. The own-words note already did that work at processing time.
items.reference:
📄 Copy-paste — the fact, stated abstractly
🗒️ Own-words — the fact, tied to a real situation and why it mattered
Why: recall speed later depends on the connection to something meaningful, not on how completely the fact was stated.

items.prompt: Both the copy-paste note and the own-words note in the L2 table are factually correct. What determines which one is actually useful later, if not correctness?
choices: Whether it's tied to something meaningful and thus fast to recall and reuse
Which one was written first
Which one is longer
Whether it uses the instructor's exact wording
items.explanation: Correctness is necessary but not sufficient — both notes clear that bar. What separates them is retrievability: whether the note is connected to something meaningful enough to be recalled and used quickly when it's needed.
items.reference:
📄 Copy-paste — the fact, stated abstractly
🗒️ Own-words — the fact, tied to a real situation and why it mattered
Why: recall speed later depends on the connection to something meaningful, not on how completely the fact was stated.

items.prompt: Why does this unit recommend processing and linking happen in a separate pass later, rather than at the exact moment of capture?
choices: Because processing at capture time slows capture down enough that the habit doesn't survive the moment it happens in
Because processed notes are less accurate than notes processed immediately
Because most note-taking tools don't allow editing a note after it's created
Because linking always requires a note to be at least a day old
items.explanation: Merging processing into the capture moment forces capture down to processing's slower pace — and capture is the step happening in moments with the least available time. Decoupling them in time lets capture stay fast while still doing the deeper work, just later.
items.reference:
⏱️ Same time — capture forced to processing's slower pace, gets skipped
🔀 Decoupled — capture stays fast, processing happens in its own short pass later
Why: the fix that survives real use separates the steps in time instead of doing everything at once.

items.prompt: This unit says an unprocessed capture backlog is 'allowed to exist briefly' but shouldn't grow forever. Why not just process every capture the same day, every day, without exception?
choices: Because a strict same-day rule can't survive the days you genuinely don't have three spare minutes, and treating it as absolute is what pushes people to abandon the system entirely rather than bend it
Because processing notes the same day they're captured makes them less accurate
Because a backlog of unprocessed notes is actually more valuable than processed ones
Because most people only capture one note per week
items.explanation: A rigid same-day rule breaks on the first busy day, and an all-or-nothing system tends to get abandoned once it's broken once. The unit's actual guidance is that a short backlog is fine as long as it doesn't grow unboundedly — this is the deliberate, sustainable version of decoupling capture from processing.
items.reference:
⏱️ Same time — capture forced to processing's slower pace, gets skipped
🔀 Decoupled — capture stays fast, processing happens in its own short pass later
Why: the fix that survives real use separates the steps in time instead of doing everything at once.

items.prompt: This unit argues the bar for adding a link between two notes should be low, even for a 'thin' or non-obvious connection. Why?
choices: Because a bad link costs almost nothing (it just sits unused), while a missed link is hard to reconstruct later once the connection is forgotten
Because more links always make a note collection faster to search, with no downside
Because thin links are usually more accurate than strong, obvious ones
Because linking software requires a minimum number of links per note to function
items.explanation: The asymmetry is the key point: a link that turns out irrelevant just sits there doing nothing, but a connection you don't record now is one you're unlikely to reconstruct later, once you've forgotten you ever thought the two ideas were related.
items.reference:
✅ Bad link added — costs nothing, just sits unused
❌ Good link missed — hard to reconstruct once the connection is forgotten
Why: the low cost of a bad link vs. the real cost of a missed one is why the bar for linking should stay low.

items.prompt: If every note in a collection ends up linked to nearly every other note, what breaks?
choices: Nothing — more links are always strictly better
The links stop meaning anything distinctive, and finding a genuinely relevant connection gets harder rather than easier
The notes app will refuse to save any more links
Processing time increases but linking stays equally useful
items.explanation: Low-cost linking has a limit: at the extreme where everything links to everything, a link no longer signals a meaningful relationship, and a genuinely useful connection gets buried among dozens of noise links. A thin link or two per note is fine; forty is a different problem.
items.reference:
✅ Bad link added — costs nothing, just sits unused
❌ Good link missed — hard to reconstruct once the connection is forgotten
Why: the low cost of a bad link vs. the real cost of a missed one is why the bar for linking should stay low.

items.prompt: Priya's actual capture during the talk was 'anchor first even if rough - Kessler??' — four words and a question mark. Why does this fragment survive a delay before processing, while a fragment like 'good point about pricing' wouldn't?
choices: Because it's grammatically correct and 'good point about pricing' isn't
Because it names something specific enough (Kessler) to reconstruct the full meaning later, while a vague fragment gives future-her nothing to anchor to
Because it's shorter, and shorter fragments are always easier to remember
Because it includes a question mark, which all good captures must include
items.explanation: The specific detail — 'Kessler' — is what lets Priya reconstruct the whole context later, even after a delay. A vague fragment has no such anchor point; by the time she'd get back to it, she'd have no way to tell which point, from which talk, it referred to.
items.reference:
✅ 'anchor first even if rough - Kessler??' — specific enough to survive a delay
❌ 'good point about pricing' — vague, won't mean anything after a delay
Why: a capture only needs to be specific enough to reconstruct later, not complete — but it does need that one anchor detail.

items.prompt: Priya's four-second capture doesn't explain what 'Kessler' means to anyone else reading it. Is that a flaw in the capture?
choices: Yes — a good capture must be understandable to any reader
No — a capture only needs to be understandable to future-her, since she's the one who'll process it later
Yes — capture should always be written for a general audience
No — captures don't need to make sense to anyone, ever, including the person who wrote them
items.explanation: The capture step's audience is future-you, not a stranger. 'Kessler' is meaningless to an outside reader but perfectly specific to Priya, and that's the only bar it needs to clear — general readability would cost more time than the capture moment allows.
items.reference:
✅ 'anchor first even if rough - Kessler??' — specific enough to survive a delay
❌ 'good point about pricing' — vague, won't mean anything after a delay
Why: a capture only needs to be specific enough to reconstruct later, not complete — but it does need that one anchor detail.

items.prompt: Under real time pressure, this unit says capture stays non-negotiable but processing can be deferred — as long as one condition holds. What's the condition?

The raw capture must include enough specific context (like a name or project) to survive the delay until it's actually processed

The note must already be linked to something before capture is considered complete
items.explanation: The deferral is safe only if the capture itself carries enough of an anchor to be reconstructed later — the time-pressure adjustment is about spending a few extra seconds making the fragment specific, not about skipping processing and hoping memory fills the gap for free.
items.reference:
✅ 'anchor first even if rough - Kessler??' — specific enough to survive a delay
❌ 'good point about pricing' — vague, won't mean anything after a delay
Why: a capture only needs to be specific enough to reconstruct later, not complete — but it does need that one anchor detail.

🏛️ Foundational — 'anchor early': process and link, it'll apply again
Why: the triage question is whether you expect to still care about the idea in six months.

items.prompt: Why does 'anchor early, even with a rough number' earn the extra processing and linking effort, while a note about a specific deploy time doesn't, even though both took the same few seconds to capture?
choices: Because the anchoring idea is more interesting to read
